client: I've been really struggling lately with this overwhelming anxiety about my final exams coming up. I got a low grade on my last psychology paper and it's been eating at me ever since, like it's proof that I'm going to fail everything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the exams are still going to happen no matter what we say in here.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — that fear that one grade has already written the ending of your story, and maybe even some doubt about whether this space can offer you anything real. I really hear that, and I want you to know that skepticism makes complete sense when you're feeling this overwhelmed. I'm curious — when you say the low grade feels like *proof* you'll fail everything, what does that voice in your head sound like, and has it ever been wrong before?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I mean... the voice is pretty loud and it basically just says "you're not smart enough, you never were, and now everyone's going to see it." It's like it's been waiting for this moment to prove itself right. And yeah, I guess it's been wrong before — like I've passed things I thought I'd fail — but somehow that never really sticks the way the bad stuff does.
therapist: That inner critic sounds relentless — like it's been collecting evidence against you for years and finally feels vindicated, while conveniently ignoring all the times you proved it wrong. What you just noticed is actually really important in CBT: our minds have a negativity bias, meaning the bad stuff tends to stick like velcro while the good stuff slides off like teflon. I'm wondering — what would it look like to deliberately make those past successes *stick* a little more, the way the failures do?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: That velcro and teflon thing actually makes a lot of sense to me, and it's kind of unsettling how accurate it is. But when you ask what it would look like to make the successes stick more... I honestly don't know, because even when I try to remind myself of good things I've done at work, my brain immediately follows up with "yeah but that was a fluke" or "anyone could have done that." It's like the critic has a counter-argument ready for everything, so I'm not sure how deliberately focusing on successes would actually change anything.
therapist: That "yeah but it was a fluke" response is actually a really well-known thinking pattern called *discounting the positive* — your critic doesn't just ignore the good stuff, it actively dismantles it before it can land. I notice you're engaging with this pretty quickly and sharply, which makes me think part of you is genuinely wrestling with it, even if another part is skeptical. What if we turned that same sharp analytical mind on the critic itself — like, what evidence would it actually take to convince you that a success *wasn't* a fluke?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, that's actually... a fair point, I guess, about the "discounting the positive" thing. But here's the problem with your question — I don't think any amount of evidence would ever fully convince me, because my brain would always find a way to poke a hole in it. Like, if I got promoted, I'd say the competition was weak; if someone praised my work, I'd say they were just being nice.
therapist: What you're describing is actually a really profound insight — that the goalposts keep moving, so no evidence ever feels like *enough*, and that's exhausting to live with. I'm curious about something though: you're laying all of this out very clearly and quickly, almost like you've thought about it a lot, and I wonder if underneath that sharp analysis there's also something that feels a bit... hopeless, or tired? Like, what does it feel like in your body when you imagine that no evidence will ever be enough?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

therapist: That heaviness in your chest — that low-grade dread — that's not just a thought, it's something your body has been holding, probably for a long time, and it takes real courage to actually notice it instead of analyzing your way around it. vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

therapist: What you just said — "always on the outside looking in, nobody actually sees you" — that's not weird at all, that's something really deep and real, and the fact that you let it land instead of immediately explaining it away is genuinely significant. client: Yeah, it... it does have a history. therapist: What you're describing — being friendly but never someone's *first choice* — that's a particular kind of loneliness that's easy to overlook because it doesn't look like isolation from the outside, but it's deeply felt on the inside. therapist: That instinct to shrink back when someone actually sees you — that makes so much sense, because being seen feels safe in theory but vulnerable in practice, especially when you've spent years protecting yourself by staying on the edges. therapist: What you just said — that being seen might prove you're not unlovable, but that terrifies you more than it comforts you — that's one of the most honest and courageous things a person can say out loud.
